means:
Ruined, withered, spoiled — struck by something that eats away at what was once healthy or promising.

The word starts in agriculture: a **blight** is a plant disease that shrivels a crop in the field. Everything else is that image applied elsewhere. So *blighted* carries three things a plain word like *ruined* doesn't: the damage **crept in from outside**, it **spread**, and the thing was **flourishing or full of promise beforehand**. A blighted career had prospects. A blighted neighbourhood had life in it. Blighted hopes were real hopes. Nothing is *blighted* if it was never going anywhere.
trap: ⚠️ **blight ≠ plight.** A **blight** is the affliction that ruins something; a **plight** is the bad situation a person is stuck in. The famine was a blight; the farmers' plight was starvation.
trick_line: **b-LIGHT-ed** — the *light* has gone out of it.
trick_unpack: Something blighted was once lit up with promise and has been slowly dimmed by an outside affliction.
sentences: Decades of factory closures left the town **blighted** — half its shopfronts boarded, its young people gone.
One bad tackle and his whole season was **blighted**.
in_the_wild: **Potato blight** caused the Irish Famine — a fungus that crept through the fields and turned a healthy staple crop black in the ground. That's the literal picture behind every figurative use.
one_line: Ruined or withered by a creeping, spreading affliction.
